cells.tense: Something new is moving in you and you're letting it come in without rushing to place it.
cells.ask: Name what's opened — a want, a warmth, a pull — in one plain sentence, out loud, before you explain it. Just hear yourself say it.
cells.core:
Carrying something heavy and staying reachable while you do it — that's the whole thing working. The weight hasn't turned you hard, and it hasn't made you cave either; things still get through to you and you're not braced against them. Plenty of people holding that much seal up to manage it, and you haven't. Whatever's arriving right now has somewhere to land.

The balance is feeding something worth keeping. You notice what lands without pouncing on it, and nothing has been stamped permanent or stamped nothing yet. Letting what you know stay open to deepening instead of settling by morning — that's the part to feed now. What's open can stay open.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy and still let something new in.
cells.verb: letting something register before you know what it is
cells.place: how you stay upright under weight

cells.tense: You're standing in the opening and racing it, already living in what this is going to be.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing you can finish in the next hour, finish it, and stop there. Let the next thing wait until it's actually here.
cells.core:
Being ready is the good version of this — you meet what's coming with a steady stance and nothing slips past you. Right now the readiness has run ahead of the thing itself. Something's starting and you've already jumped to what it will need, what it will mean, how you'll handle it, so the feeling that's actually here doesn't get its turn. You're gripping a version that hasn't arrived, and the grip wears the thing down before it can.

Preparation isn't the problem; it's one of the ways you keep from getting knocked over. Pushed this far it stops being readiness and turns into rehearsal. Finishing one thing pulls you back to where the opening actually happens, which is now.
cells.sheetLine: You're preparing for a moment that hasn't started yet.

cells.tense: Something's been opening in you and you've kept your distance from it, the way you learned to somewhere you've already left.
cells.ask: Take sixty seconds with a window, a plant, or your own hands — nothing to do, nothing to learn. Let your attention land on one thing and stay there until the time's up.
cells.core:
When this holds well, you carry a heavy load and still feel small new things land — a warm meal going in, an offhand kindness registering, the first cool minute of an evening. The weight and the warmth sit side by side; nothing has to give for the other to happen.

Right now you're holding your own, staying useful, staying steady, and somewhere in all that carrying the new thing stopped getting a turn. It isn't that you can't feel it. You've stopped showing up for it.

A minute of plain attention tells you whether that's still true. Receiving doesn't wait on you lifting less; it rides on the same strength you're already using.
cells.sheetLine: You're standing right at the opening and waiting outside it.

cells.tense: You're already letting something in — reading it, feeling your way — and calling it just being careful.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to no one, 'this is me letting it in,' about one time in the last day you waited before deciding. Do it once, plainly, and leave it at that.
cells.core:
You read what moves in you the way you read a room — you catch your own response before you name it, and you wait before deciding. That's the opening already doing its work. You've just been calling it caution, or keeping your head, or not making a thing of it. What's running is fine. What's missing is any claim on it.

That's good news: the ground is already there. When a moment of waiting gets seen as a moment of receiving, the whole thing simplifies — the feeling doesn't need to be right, you just tell the truth about whose it is.

attempts.check: The one thing not in the record is what the person feels about the opening itself — whether it's welcome, inconvenient, or already happening and being used, so no cell claims their attitude toward it, only what the capacity is doing. A reader might say the tied-to-others line in Too Much implicates people in a way the record doesn't, and they could be right, so the mechanism is kept to staying ahead of timing, which is what DIAGONAL in excess actually names. The asks survive being wrong because each one is a small sensory wager — something a person can try for an hour and learn from even if the seat is the wrong one. The line that would serve the writer more than the reader is any sentence about the opening being the whole story; it's been kept out, because the point of these cells is what keeps a person standing, and the opening is something they carry, not something they become.
